comments: > Since I am not an expert on number theory, all this is very tentative and I could be making serious mistakes.Seems like an important caveat to highlight here.I feel a lot of concern for Masullo in this situation. If the journey does not engage or enrich you, it is already a fool’s errand right at the first step.I hope he is already a more skillful and insightful mathematician because of the struggles he had to go through and he will have better insight than most to scope new problems to work on. The other, by Alessandro Masullo, is a 940-page human-written manuscript that Ravi Vakil posted on his blog:• Ravi Vakil, Hurried announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH, Math 216 blog, November 20, 2026.• Alessandro Maria Masullo, The Music of the Primes, draft, November 20, 2026.While there’s been an enormous outpouring about the drama of this situation, so far it’s hard to find good simple accounts of Masullo’s paper. > The bitter lesson has so far never failed usI'm not sure what you are saying here, because the bitter lesson is this:One thing that should be learned from the bitter lesson is the great power of general purpose methods, of methods that continue to scale with increased computation even as the available computation becomes very great. The two methods that seem to scale arbitrarily in this way are search and learning.There's nothing here that pushes particularly hard for remote computer: Yes, we probably aren't going to be training our own models from scratch locally for a while, but running a heavily trained model locally is an entirely valid application of the bitter lesson.Indeed, there are ways to apply the bitter lesson that would work better locally than remotely. For example, learnt LORA extensions could allow local preferences to be learnt and used much better than in a remote setup.Having said that, I agree there will be huge demand for remote models: It's easy, they are fast, there is less up front investment from the user, etc etc.reply

title: GL.iNet Security Notice 2026-11-20 (gl-inet.com)
comments: Dump all this cloud-connected garbage, flash OpenWrt or build your own router using an old PC or laptop. No home appliance should connect to any remote service.reply

Vanilla OpenWrt is not necessarily more secure than a vendor fork (though dropping the cloud/remote-access layer obviously reduces the attack surface). It really depends on the build and config options.For example, by default:- The web UI serves plaintext HTTP and doesn't redirect to HTTPS. [1]- The router generates a persistent DUID from its LAN MAC and sends it to your ISP. [2][3]- Userspace is FORTIFY_SOURCE=1 and PIE/ASLR are not enabled on all binaries. BusyBox (which runs the WAN DHCP and NTP clients) isn't built with PIE unless you set PKG_ASLR_PIE_ALL. [4]There are other defaults and unneeded packages that can be changed or removed. I spent a lot of time tuning the configs and switching some daemons to Rust before ultimately deciding that a NixOS gateway + separate AP was more viable.[1] https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt/blob/main/package/network...[2] https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt/blob/main/package/base-fi...[3] https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt/blob/main/package/network...[4] https://github.com/openwrt/openwrt/blob/main/config/Config-b...reply

title: The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge [pdf] (1939) (ias.edu)
comments: A couple points:1. Random knowledge can often be used to build a "map" to conclusions that turn out to be usefule.g. someone once asked me what what country was number 2 in terms of total airplane flights (the US is number 1).I deduced:- had to be a big country- with spread out cities- and required flying instead of drivingI remembered reading that Brazil has traffic that is so bad and such poor security that people commute to work via helicopter. Even though I wasn't sure it was Brazil, I could guesstimate that it was indeed Brazil.2. Random facts are great for creating shared references or metaphors across cultural or organizational boundaries.e.g. I worked with many people from India over the years and being able to quote a famous Bollywood movie or Indian mythology was excellent at helping build rapport etc3. I was watching a documentary on an Army jungle survival school. The instructor mentioned:"People ask me if they should read survival guides or biographies of people who survived a calamity. I 100% say yes b/c the after action reports of people surviving are filled with stories of 'then I remembered this random fact from years ago that helped me survive'."reply
On your first point, the actual answer appears to be China? Brazil is second in general aviation fleet size and airport count, if you meant one of those.reply

Knowing random facts about countries and capitals and some of the better known events or works of art is not just a party trick, it can help you explain other future events. title: What we learned operating auth for 1k APIs (nango.dev)
comments: Even `expires_in` requires care.  The token expires in 3600s, but, from when?  In the token there will be an `exp` with an absolute value, but `expires_in` in the envelope is relative -- relative to when?  Relative to whenever the issuer issued the token, so relative to `iat`/`exp`.  But you don't want to have to extract that from the token, and you won't get to if the token is encrypted, so the best you can do is add `expires_in` to now, but it has to be a clock value from before you send the request.reply
